I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Mexico City, Mexico at 2026-12-31 07:28 CST (UTC-0600) (2026-12-31T13:28:00Z in UTC), at latitude 19.4326 degrees and longitude -99.1332 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 3.194 degrees and its azimuth is 115.746 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 57.833 degrees and its azimuth is 193.118 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 42.2 percent illuminated, 80.868 degrees from the Sun, and 383809.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **It will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to see the Moon with the naked eye.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the specific conditions you described:

### 1. The "Daylight" Factor (The Biggest Obstacle)
You mentioned the sky brightness is **"bright daylight."** This is the primary reason you likely won't see it. 
*   Even though the Moon is high in the sky (at an altitude of nearly 58 degrees), the Sun is also above the horizon (at 3.19 degrees). 
*   When the Sun is up, the atmosphere scatters blue light so effectively that it creates a "veil" of brightness. To see the Moon during the day, it usually needs to be very close to a Full Moon phase (where it reflects the maximum amount of light) or very close to the horizon where the atmosphere might provide some contrast.

### 2. The Phase and Illumination
The Moon is only **42.2% illuminated**. 
*   A "Waxing Gibbous" moon at this illumination level is significantly dimmer than a Full Moon. 
*   Because it is not fully illuminated, it doesn't have the "brilliance" required to punch through the glare of a daylight sky.

### 3. The Geometry (The "Look" Direction)
*   **The Sun** is at an azimuth of **115.7°** (East-Southeast).
*   **The Moon** is at an azimuth of **193.1°** (South-Southwest).
*   This means the Moon is about 77 degrees away from the Sun in the sky. While they aren't right next to each other, the Moon is still "in the neighborhood" of the Sun's glare. Because the Moon is 42% lit, it won't have the high contrast needed to stand out against the bright blue of the daytime sky.

### The Verdict
If you were looking at a **Full Moon** at that altitude during the day, you would have a very good chance of seeing it. However, because it is only **42% illuminated**, it will likely be "washed out" by the brightness of the atmosphere.

**Your best bet:** If you have a pair of **binoculars**, you would almost certainly be able to see it! The magnification would help pull the Moon's shape out from the bright background of the sky. Without them, it will likely be invisible to the naked eye.
